units.name: Numbers and Place Value
units.summary: What each digit in a number is worth, and how to compare numbers.

units.name: Multiplication and Division
units.summary: Working with equal groups, and sharing things out fairly.

topics.name: Place Value to Thousands
topics.summary: Why the 5 in 500 is worth more than the 5 in 50.

topics.name: Multiplication
topics.summary: A faster way to add the same number many times.

objectives.text: Say what each digit in a number is worth.
Write a number in expanded form.
Compare two numbers and say which is bigger.

keyTerms.definition: What a digit is worth because of where it sits in the number.
A number written as the sum of what each digit is worth.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: The same digit can be worth very different amounts. By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at any number up to 9999 and say exactly what each digit is worth.

sections.heading: The same digit, different value
sections.body:
Look at these two numbers:

    50        500

Both have a 5. But they are not the same.

In 50, the 5 means five tens. That is 50.
In 500, the 5 means five hundreds. That is 500.

The 5 did not change. Its POSITION changed. That is the whole idea of place value: where a digit sits tells you what it is worth.

sections.heading: The four places
sections.body:
For numbers up to 9999 there are four places. Reading from the right:

    Thousands | Hundreds | Tens | Ones

Take the number 3472:

    3 is in the thousands place → 3000
    4 is in the hundreds place  → 400
    7 is in the tens place      → 70
    2 is in the ones place      → 2

Add them up: 3000 + 400 + 70 + 2 = 3472. That is where the number comes from.
sections.example:
Writing 2605 in expanded form.

Start from the left and name each place:

    2 thousands = 2000
    6 hundreds  = 600
    0 tens      = 0
    5 ones      = 5

So 2605 = 2000 + 600 + 0 + 5

The zero matters. It is holding the tens place open. Without it you would write 265, which is a completely different number.

sections.heading: Comparing numbers
sections.body:
To compare two numbers, do not look at the whole thing at once. Start from the LEFT and compare one place at a time.

Which is bigger, 4218 or 4231?

    Thousands: 4 and 4. The same. Keep going.
    Hundreds:  2 and 2. The same. Keep going.
    Tens:      1 and 3. Different! 3 is bigger.

So 4231 is bigger. You can stop there — once you find a difference, the rest does not matter.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. What is the 7 worth in 4700?
2. Write 5083 in expanded form. Be careful with the zero.
3. Which is bigger, 3990 or 3909? Compare one place at a time.
4. I am a number. I have 6 hundreds, 0 tens and 4 ones. What number am I?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A digit is worth different amounts in different places.
• The four places are thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.
• Expanded form shows what each digit is worth, added together.
• Zero holds a place open. Do not leave it out.
• To compare, start from the left and stop at the first difference.

objectives.text: Explain multiplication as adding equal groups.
Write a multiplication sentence from a picture or story.
Use the fact that order does not change the answer.

keyTerms.definition: To add the same number a certain number of times.
The answer you get when you multiply.
Groups that all have the same number in them.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Multiplication is not a new kind of maths. It is a faster way of doing addition you already know.

sections.heading: Where multiplication comes from
sections.body:
A woman sells mangoes in piles. Each pile has 4 mangoes. She has 3 piles.

How many mangoes altogether?

You could add:

    4 + 4 + 4 = 12

That works. But if she had 30 piles, adding 4 thirty times would take a long time.

So instead we write:

    3 × 4 = 12

Read it as "3 groups of 4". The × sign means "groups of". Multiplication is just a short way of writing repeated addition.

sections.heading: Reading the two numbers
sections.body:
In 3 × 4 = 12:

    3 tells you HOW MANY groups
    4 tells you HOW MANY are in each group
    12 is the answer, called the product

Every group must have the SAME amount. If one pile had 4 mangoes and another had 5, you could not multiply — you would have to add.
sections.example:
A story into a multiplication sentence.

"Five children each carry 6 stones. How many stones altogether?"

Step 1 — How many groups? There are 5 children, so 5 groups.
Step 2 — How many in each group? 6 stones each.
Step 3 — Write it:

    5 × 6 = 30

Step 4 — Check by adding:
    6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30 ✓

Thirty stones.

sections.heading: Order does not matter
sections.body:
Here is something useful:

    3 × 4 = 12
    4 × 3 = 12

The answer is the same both ways.

Picture it. Three rows of four dots:

    • • • •
    • • • •
    • • • •

Now turn the picture on its side. It becomes four rows of three. The dots did not move — you only looked from a different direction. So the total cannot change.

This is genuinely useful. If you know 2 × 9, you already know 9 × 2. Learning one fact gives you two.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Write 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 as a multiplication sentence, then find the answer.
2. There are 8 desks. Each desk has 2 pupils. How many pupils?
3. If you know 6 × 5 = 30, what is 5 × 6? How do you know without working it out?
4. Draw 4 rows of 3 dots. How many dots? Now turn your paper sideways. What multiplication does it show?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Multiplication is repeated addition of EQUAL groups.
• In 3 × 4, the 3 is how many groups and the 4 is how many in each.
• The answer is called the product.
• Order does not change the answer: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3.
• If the groups are not equal, you must add instead.

questions.question: In the number 4700, what is the 7 worth?
questions.explanation: The 7 sits in the hundreds place, so it is worth 7 hundreds, which is 700. If you chose 7, you read the digit on its own instead of looking at where it sits. Where a digit sits is what gives it its value.

questions.question: Which of these is 2605 written in expanded form?
questions.explanation: 2605 has 2 thousands, 6 hundreds, 0 tens and 5 ones, so it is 2000 + 600 + 0 + 5, which we write as 2000 + 600 + 5. The zero adds nothing, but it still holds the tens place open — without it in the original number you would have 265, which is far smaller.

questions.question: Which number is bigger: 3990 or 3909?
questions.explanation: Compare from the left, one place at a time. Thousands: 3 and 3, the same. Hundreds: 9 and 9, the same. Tens: 9 and 0 — different, and 9 is bigger. So 3990 is bigger. Once you find a difference you can stop; the ones place cannot change the answer.

questions.question: Which multiplication sentence means the same as 7 + 7 + 7 + 7?
questions.explanation: There are four 7s being added, so it is 4 groups of 7, written 4 × 7 = 28. Choosing 7 × 7 counts seven groups, but only four are written down. Count how many times the number appears — that is the first number.

questions.question: There are 8 desks. Each desk has 2 pupils. How many pupils altogether?
questions.explanation: 8 groups of 2 is 8 × 2 = 16 pupils. Choosing 10 means you added 8 + 2 instead of multiplying. The words "each desk has" tell you the groups are equal, and equal groups mean multiply.

questions.question: You know that 6 × 5 = 30. Without working it out, what is 5 × 6?
questions.explanation: It is 30. Order does not change the answer in multiplication. Picture 6 rows of 5 dots, then turn the paper sideways — it becomes 5 rows of 6, and no dots were added or taken away. This is useful: every fact you learn gives you a second one free.
